title: Work out daily? OK, but how socially fit are you?
excerpt: Harvard Study of Adult Development director details what research says about value of relationships to physical and mental health.
content_html:
Robert Waldinger, director of the Harvard Study of Adult Development, says one of the biggest surprises they encountered was that what makes people happy is also what helps keep them healthy — relationships. The research project, the longest in-depth study of physical and mental well-being among adults, began in 1938 with 724 participants: 268 Harvard College sophomores and 456 young adults from Boston. It now includes 1,300 descendants of its original participants. The Gazette spoke with Waldinger about his new book, “The Good Life,” which he co-wrote with Marc Schulz. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Q&A

Robert Waldinger

GAZETTE: One of the conclusions of your book involves how key good relationships are to both physical as well as mental well-being. Were researchers expecting that to be true?

WALDINGER: As part of the study, we followed our first generation of participants through their entire adult lives — from teenage years all the way into old age. When they reached age 80, we realized we had all these data about their physical and mental health, which we had collected year after year after year.

We started wondering whether we could look back at our participants’ lives in middle age and see what the biggest predictors were of who’s going to be happy and healthy by age 80. We thought that cholesterol level or blood pressure at age 50 would be more important. They were not. It was satisfaction in their relationships, particularly in their marriages, that was the best predictor of a happy and healthy life.

At first, we didn’t believe it; we were wondering how this could be possible. We thought, “It makes sense that if you have happy relationships, you’ll be happier, but how could the quality of your relationships make it more or less likely that you would get coronary artery disease or Type 2 diabetes or arthritis?” We thought maybe this isn’t a real finding, maybe it’s by chance. Then other research groups began to find the same thing. Now it is a very robust finding. It’s very well established that interpersonal connectedness, and the quality of those connections, really impact health, as well as happiness.

“[I]f you are alone and feel stressed and lonely, that’s part of what breaks down your health. That’s why we think loneliness is as dangerous to your health as smoking half a pack of cigarettes a day or being obese.”

GAZETTE: Is there solid medical evidence that supports how good relationships might affect physical health?

WALDINGER: Some people might think this finding is very touchy-feely, right? The question you are asking is exactly what researchers were asking, which is, “How does that work? What would the mechanism be by which relationships affect physiology?” We have spent the last 10 years in our lab studying this. The best hypothesis for which there are good data suggests that it is about stress and the regulation of stress by our relationships.

First, stress is a natural part of life. It happens every day to most of us: Something will come along that will stress us, and when that happens, the body goes into fight-or-flight mode. When that happens, you can feel your heart rate increase, your blood pressure goes up, you might start to sweat, and that’s normal because we want the body to prepare itself to meet a challenge. But when the challenge is removed, we want the body to go back to equilibrium. For example, if I have something upsetting happen during the day, and I’m churning or ruminating about it, I go home and talk to my wife or a friend, and if that person is a good listener, I can literally feel my body calm down.

But if you don’t have anyone like that, and many people don’t, if you are isolated or you don’t have a confidant, what we think happens is that the body stays in a kind of low-level fight-or-flight mode, and that means that there are higher levels of circulating stress hormones and higher levels of inflammation, and those things can gradually wear away many body systems. That’s how we think stress can wear down multiple body systems and how good relationships can be protective of our health.

GAZETTE: How about career and financial success? Are they as important as good relationships?

WALDINGER: Certainly, having a job you enjoy or care about and find meaningful is important. Having a job you hate lowers your well-being for sure. But what we know from good studies is that wealth does not increase well-being significantly once we have our basic needs met. Once you get beyond basic financial security, your happiness doesn’t go up very much.

Similarly, fame or high achievement — becoming a Harvard professor or winning the Nobel Prize — won’t make you happier. Maybe the work that got you the Nobel Prize is meaningful to you, and that can make you happy. But the badges of achievement and the badges of wealth don’t make people happy. That’s important to keep in mind because we tell each other a lot of stories about what’s going to make us happy. We get these messages all day long from ads that convey the message that if you just buy this thing, you’ll be happier, or they show people living these beautiful and wealthy lives, and that’s the key to a happy life. It turns out that’s not true.

“What we see in our research is that everybody needs at least one solid relationship, someone whom they feel they can count on in times of need.”

GAZETTE: Your book highlights the importance of having good relationships with your parents, siblings, neighbors, coworkers, even acquaintances. Can you expand on that?

WALDINGER: There’s no set number of connections you need to have. If you have everything you need in your family, that’s great. Maybe, you don’t need a wider circle. But what we find is that the benefits of relationships come from anywhere. They certainly come from family, but they can come from friends, from work colleagues, and we even get small bits of well-being from a chat with the person who makes coffee for us in the coffee shop or from a chat with the cashier who checks us out in the grocery store, or the mail carrier. If we have pleasant connections with those people, those also contribute to our well-being.

Some of us are more shy, and some of us are more extroverted. Shy people need fewer relationships whereas an extrovert needs more. What we see in our research is that everybody needs at least one solid relationship, someone whom they feel they can count on in times of need. In one of our questionnaires, we asked our participants, “Who could you call in the middle of the night, if you were sick or scared? List everybody.” Most people could list several people, but some people, even some who were married, couldn’t list anyone. We think that everybody needs at least one person that you know would be there for you.

“Our social life is a living system, and it needs maintenance too. One of the ways you can do it is through tiny actions.”

GAZETTE: What is the impact of loneliness on your physical health? In your book you write that loneliness could be as dangerous to your health as smoking or being obese.

WALDINGER: We think that it operates through this mechanism of chronic stress — that loneliness is a stressor. We evolved to be social creatures because it was safer to be in a group. If you think about when we were trying to survive out in the wilderness, you realize that people who banded together survived longer. We hypothesize that there was genetic selection for being more social. Being alone is a stressor; being isolated is a stressor. Many people feel chronically unsafe when they are lonely. If you’re alone and you’re content, that’s different. But if you are alone and feel stressed and lonely, that’s part of what breaks down your health. That’s why we think loneliness is as dangerous to your health as smoking half a pack of cigarettes a day or being obese. Loneliness has a similar physiologic fingerprint as those other two problems.

GAZETTE: What if people feel it’s too late in life to have good relationships?

WALDINGER: What we find in following thousands of people is that many people who thought it was too late for them, who thought, “I’m no good at relationships,” found relationships at a time when they didn’t expect to. We have a story in the book of one man who retired. He didn’t have a good marriage, and he never had friends. He joined a gym, and he found a group of friends who became his tribe, and they started socializing together. And he wrote to us that he was happy in a way he had never been because he had these people in his life. We find people who find love in their 70s and 80s who never expected it. Based on our science, we can say that it’s never too late. And if you think you’re never going to have good relationships, you don’t know that for sure. It’s worth the effort. People can make an effort.

GAZETTE: What steps should people take to start working on building good relationships?

WALDINGER: We talk in the book about what we call “social fitness.” The reason we call it that is to frame it as analogous to physical fitness. We think of physical fitness as a practice, as something we do to maintain our bodies. Our social life is a living system, and it needs maintenance too. One of the ways you can do it is through tiny actions. You could think right now, “Whom do I miss? Who would I like to see more of? Who haven’t I been in touch with?” and send them a text, an email, or call them on the phone. You will be amazed at the positive responses that you get for this tiny action.

The piece of advice I’d like to give is that there are some small actions we can take to enliven our social world. The other thing is to think about how you could make new connections, and probably one of the easiest ways to do that is to do something you care about or enjoy doing and do it alongside other people. It could be a bowling league, a gardening club, a knitting group, a political campaign, or working to prevent climate change. Just remember that when you do something you care about in a group, you already have something in common with the people you’re with. It’s a natural place to start conversations, and what we find is that when people repeatedly have casual contact with the same people, that’s the easiest place to start deepening relationships.

One last point I want to make is that nobody is happy all the time. That’s important to know because we can end up believing that if we’re not happy all the time, we’re doing something wrong. No life is happy all the time. Every life is filled with challenge and hard times. This idea about strengthening relationships is a way to increase our happiness, but also to build a safety net that helps us weather those hard times that all of us have in our lives.

When that happens, you can feel your heart rate increase, your blood pressure goes up, you might start to sweat, and that’s normal because we want the body to prepare itself to meet a challenge. But when the challenge is removed, we want the body to go back to equilibrium. For example, if I have something upsetting happen during the day, and I’m churning or ruminating about it, I go home and talk to my wife or a friend, and if that person is a good listener, I can literally feel my body calm down.

sentences.en: First, stress is a natural part of life.
sentences.zh: 首先，压力是生活中自然的一部分。

sentences.en: It happens every day to most of us: Something will come along that will stress us, and when that happens, the body goes into fight-or-flight mode.
sentences.zh: 对于我们大多数人来说，这种情况每天都会发生：某些事情会给我们带来压力，当这种情况发生时，身体就会进入战斗或逃跑模式。

sentences.en: When that happens, you can feel your heart rate increase, your blood pressure goes up, you might start to sweat, and that’s normal because we want the body to prepare itself to meet a challenge.
sentences.zh: 当这种情况发生时，您会感觉到心率加快，血压升高，您可能会开始出汗，这是正常的，因为我们希望身体做好准备迎接挑战。

sentences.en: But when the challenge is removed, we want the body to go back to equilibrium.
sentences.zh: 但当挑战消除后，我们希望身体恢复平衡。

sentences.en: For example, if I have something upsetting happen during the day, and I’m churning or ruminating about it, I go home and talk to my wife or a friend, and if that person is a good listener, I can literally feel my body calm down.
sentences.zh: 例如，如果我白天发生了一些令人不安的事情，而我正在翻腾或沉思，我就会回家和我的妻子或朋友交谈，如果那个人是一个好的倾听者，我真的可以感觉到我的身体平静下来。

blocks.html_en: But if you don’t have anyone like that, and many people don’t, if you are isolated or you don’t have a confidant, what we think happens is that the body stays in a kind of low-level fight-or-flight mode, and that means that there are higher levels of circulating stress hormones and higher levels of inflammation, and those things can gradually wear away many body systems. That’s how we think stress can wear down multiple body systems and how good relationships can be protective of our health.

sentences.en: But if you don’t have anyone like that, and many people don’t, if you are isolated or you don’t have a confidant, what we think happens is that the body stays in a kind of low-level fight-or-flight mode, and that means that there are higher levels of circulating stress hormones and higher levels of inflammation, and those things can gradually wear away many body systems.
sentences.zh: 但如果你没有这样的人，很多人也没有，如果你被孤立或者没有知己，我们认为会发生的情况是身体处于一种低水平的战斗或逃跑模式，这意味着循环压力激素水平更高，炎症水平更高，这些东西会逐渐磨损许多身体系统。

sentences.en: That’s how we think stress can wear down multiple body systems and how good relationships can be protective of our health.
sentences.zh: 这就是我们认为压力会削弱多个身体系统的原因，也是良好的人际关系可以保护我们健康的原因。

blocks.html_en: GAZETTE: How about career and financial success? Are they as important as good relationships?

sentences.en: GAZETTE: How about career and financial success?
sentences.zh: 公报：职业和财务上的成功怎么样？

sentences.en: Are they as important as good relationships?
sentences.zh: 它们和良好的关系一样重要吗？

blocks.html_en: WALDINGER: Certainly, having a job you enjoy or care about and find meaningful is important. Having a job you hate lowers your well-being for sure. But what we know from good studies is that wealth does not increase well-being significantly once we have our basic needs met. Once you get beyond basic financial security, your happiness doesn’t go up very much.

sentences.en: WALDINGER: Certainly, having a job you enjoy or care about and find meaningful is important.
sentences.zh: 沃尔丁格：当然，拥有一份自己喜欢或关心并且觉得有意义的工作很重要。

sentences.en: Having a job you hate lowers your well-being for sure.
sentences.zh: 从事你讨厌的工作肯定会降低你的幸福感。

sentences.en: But what we know from good studies is that wealth does not increase well-being significantly once we have our basic needs met.
sentences.zh: 但我们从良好的研究中得知，一旦我们的基本需求得到满足，财富就不会显着增加幸福感。

sentences.en: Once you get beyond basic financial security, your happiness doesn’t go up very much.
sentences.zh: 一旦你超出了基本的财务保障，你的幸福感就不会增加太多。

blocks.html_en: Similarly, fame or high achievement — becoming a Harvard professor or winning the Nobel Prize — won’t make you happier. Maybe the work that got you the Nobel Prize is meaningful to you, and that can make you happy. But the badges of achievement and the badges of wealth don’t make people happy. That’s important to keep in mind because we tell each other a lot of stories about what’s going to make us happy. We get these messages all day long from ads that convey the message that if you just buy this thing, you’ll be happier, or they show people living these beautiful and wealthy lives, and that’s the key to a happy life. It turns out that’s not true.

sentences.en: Similarly, fame or high achievement — becoming a Harvard professor or winning the Nobel Prize — won’t make you happier.
sentences.zh: 同样，名声或成就——成为哈佛大学教授或获得诺贝尔奖——也不会让你更快乐。

sentences.en: Maybe the work that got you the Nobel Prize is meaningful to you, and that can make you happy.
sentences.zh: 也许让你获得诺贝尔奖的工作对你来说很有意义，可以让你开心。

sentences.en: But the badges of achievement and the badges of wealth don’t make people happy.
sentences.zh: 但成就徽章和财富徽章并不会让人们感到快乐。

sentences.en: That’s important to keep in mind because we tell each other a lot of stories about what’s going to make us happy.
sentences.zh: 记住这一点很重要，因为我们会互相讲很多让我们快乐的故事。

sentences.en: We get these messages all day long from ads that convey the message that if you just buy this thing, you’ll be happier, or they show people living these beautiful and wealthy lives, and that’s the key to a happy life.
sentences.zh: 我们整天从广告中收到这些信息，这些广告传达的信息是，如果你买这个东西，你就会更快乐，或者它们展示了人们过着美好而富裕的生活，这是幸福生活的关键。

sentences.en: It turns out that’s not true.
sentences.zh: 事实证明这不是真的。

blocks.html_en: “What we see in our research is that everybody needs at least one solid relationship, someone whom they feel they can count on in times of need.”

sentences.en: “What we see in our research is that everybody needs at least one solid relationship, someone whom they feel they can count on in times of need.”
sentences.zh: “我们在研究中发现，每个人都需要至少一种牢固的关系，他们觉得在需要的时候可以依靠的人。”

blocks.html_en: “What we see in our research is that everybody needs at least one solid relationship, someone whom they feel they can count on in times of need.”

sentences.en: “What we see in our research is that everybody needs at least one solid relationship, someone whom they feel they can count on in times of need.”
sentences.zh: “我们在研究中发现，每个人都需要至少一种牢固的关系，他们觉得在需要的时候可以依靠的人。”

blocks.html_en: GAZETTE: Your book highlights the importance of having good relationships with your parents, siblings, neighbors, coworkers, even acquaintances. Can you expand on that?

sentences.en: GAZETTE: Your book highlights the importance of having good relationships with your parents, siblings, neighbors, coworkers, even acquaintances.
sentences.zh: 公报：你的书强调了与父母、兄弟姐妹、邻居、同事甚至熟人保持良好关系的重要性。

sentences.en: Can you expand on that?
sentences.zh: 你能扩展一下吗？

blocks.html_en: WALDINGER: There’s no set number of connections you need to have. If you have everything you need in your family, that’s great. Maybe, you don’t need a wider circle. But what we find is that the benefits of relationships come from anywhere. They certainly come from family, but they can come from friends, from work colleagues, and we even get small bits of well-being from a chat with the person who makes coffee for us in the coffee shop or from a chat with the cashier who checks us out in the grocery store, or the mail carrier. If we have pleasant connections with those people, those also contribute to our well-being.

sentences.en: WALDINGER: There’s no set number of connections you need to have.
sentences.zh: WALDINGER：您需要拥有的连接数量没有规定。

sentences.en: If you have everything you need in your family, that’s great.
sentences.zh: 如果您拥有家人所需的一切，那就太好了。

sentences.en: Maybe, you don’t need a wider circle.
sentences.zh: 也许，你不需要更广阔的圈子。

sentences.en: But what we find is that the benefits of relationships come from anywhere.
sentences.zh: 但我们发现，关系的好处来自任何地方。

sentences.en: They certainly come from family, but they can come from friends, from work colleagues, and we even get small bits of well-being from a chat with the person who makes coffee for us in the coffee shop or from a chat with the cashier who checks us out in the grocery store, or the mail carrier.
sentences.zh: 它们当然来自家人，但也可以来自朋友、同事，我们甚至可以通过与咖啡店里为我们煮咖啡的人聊天，或者与杂货店结账的收银员或邮递员聊天来获得一点点幸福感。

sentences.en: If we have pleasant connections with those people, those also contribute to our well-being.
sentences.zh: 如果我们与这些人有愉快的联系，这些也会对我们的福祉做出贡献。

blocks.html_en: Some of us are more shy, and some of us are more extroverted. Shy people need fewer relationships whereas an extrovert needs more. What we see in our research is that everybody needs at least one solid relationship, someone whom they feel they can count on in times of need. In one of our questionnaires, we asked our participants, “Who could you call in the middle of the night, if you were sick or scared? List everybody.” Most people could list several people, but some people, even some who were married, couldn’t list anyone. We think that everybody needs at least one person that you know would be there for you.

sentences.en: Some of us are more shy, and some of us are more extroverted.
sentences.zh: 我们中的一些人比较害羞，而另一些人则比较外向。

sentences.en: Shy people need fewer relationships whereas an extrovert needs more.
sentences.zh: 害羞的人需要​​较少的人际关系，而外向的人则需要更多的人际关系。

sentences.en: What we see in our research is that everybody needs at least one solid relationship, someone whom they feel they can count on in times of need.
sentences.zh: 我们在研究中发现，每个人都需要至少一种牢固的关系，他们认为在需要时可以依靠的人。

sentences.en: In one of our questionnaires, we asked our participants, “Who could you call in the middle of the night, if you were sick or scared?
sentences.zh: 在我们的一份调查问卷中，我们问参与者：“如果你生病或害怕了，你可以在半夜打电话给谁？

sentences.en: List everybody.”
sentences.zh: 把所有人都列出来。”

sentences.en: Most people could list several people, but some people, even some who were married, couldn’t list anyone.
sentences.zh: 大多数人可以列出几个人，但有些人，甚至有些已婚的人，无法列出任何人。

sentences.en: We think that everybody needs at least one person that you know would be there for you.
sentences.zh: 我们认为每个人都至少需要一个你知道会在你身边的人。

blocks.html_en: “Our social life is a living system, and it needs maintenance too. One of the ways you can do it is through tiny actions.”

sentences.en: “Our social life is a living system, and it needs maintenance too.
sentences.zh: “我们的社会生活是一个生命系统，也需要维护。

sentences.en: One of the ways you can do it is through tiny actions.”
sentences.zh: 做到这一点的方法之一就是通过微小的行动。”

blocks.html_en: GAZETTE: What is the impact of loneliness on your physical health? In your book you write that loneliness could be as dangerous to your health as smoking or being obese.

sentences.en: GAZETTE: What is the impact of loneliness on your physical health?
sentences.zh: 公报：孤独对您的身体健康有何影响？

sentences.en: In your book you write that loneliness could be as dangerous to your health as smoking or being obese.
sentences.zh: 您在书中写道，孤独对您的健康可能与吸烟或肥胖一样危险。

blocks.html_en: WALDINGER: We think that it operates through this mechanism of chronic stress — that loneliness is a stressor. We evolved to be social creatures because it was safer to be in a group. If you think about when we were trying to survive out in the wilderness, you realize that people who banded together survived longer. We hypothesize that there was genetic selection for being more social. Being alone is a stressor; being isolated is a stressor. Many people feel chronically unsafe when they are lonely. If you’re alone and you’re content, that’s different. But if you are alone and feel stressed and lonely, that’s part of what breaks down your health. That’s why we think loneliness is as dangerous to your health as smoking half a pack of cigarettes a day or being obese. Loneliness has a similar physiologic fingerprint as those other two problems.

sentences.en: WALDINGER: We think that it operates through this mechanism of chronic stress — that loneliness is a stressor.
sentences.zh: 沃尔丁格：我们认为它是通过这种慢性压力机制发挥作用的——孤独是一种压力源。

sentences.en: We evolved to be social creatures because it was safer to be in a group.
sentences.zh: 我们进化成为社会生物，因为在群体中更安全。

sentences.en: If you think about when we were trying to survive out in the wilderness, you realize that people who banded together survived longer.
sentences.zh: 如果你想想当我们试图在荒野中生存时，你就会意识到团结起来的人们能活得更久。

sentences.en: We hypothesize that there was genetic selection for being more social.
sentences.zh: 我们假设基因选择是为了变得更加社交。

sentences.en: Being alone is a stressor; being isolated is a stressor.
sentences.zh: 独处是一种压力源；被孤立是一种压力源。

sentences.en: Many people feel chronically unsafe when they are lonely.
sentences.zh: 许多人在孤独时会长期感到不安全。

sentences.en: If you’re alone and you’re content, that’s different.
sentences.zh: 如果你独自一人并且感到满足，那就不同了。

sentences.en: But if you are alone and feel stressed and lonely, that’s part of what breaks down your health.
sentences.zh: 但如果你独自一人并感到压力和孤独，这就是破坏你健康的部分原因。

sentences.en: That’s why we think loneliness is as dangerous to your health as smoking half a pack of cigarettes a day or being obese.
sentences.zh: 这就是为什么我们认为孤独对健康的危害与每天吸半包烟或肥胖一样危险。

sentences.en: Loneliness has a similar physiologic fingerprint as those other two problems.
sentences.zh: 孤独与其他两个问题有着相似的生理特征。

blocks.html_en: GAZETTE: What if people feel it’s too late in life to have good relationships?

sentences.en: GAZETTE: What if people feel it’s too late in life to have good relationships?
sentences.zh: 公报：如果人们觉得在生命中建立良好的人际关系为时已晚怎么办？

blocks.html_en: WALDINGER: What we find in following thousands of people is that many people who thought it was too late for them, who thought, “I’m no good at relationships,” found relationships at a time when they didn’t expect to. We have a story in the book of one man who retired. He didn’t have a good marriage, and he never had friends. He joined a gym, and he found a group of friends who became his tribe, and they started socializing together. And he wrote to us that he was happy in a way he had never been because he had these people in his life. We find people who find love in their 70s and 80s who never expected it. Based on our science, we can say that it’s never too late. And if you think you’re never going to have good relationships, you don’t know that for sure. It’s worth the effort. People can make an effort.

sentences.en: WALDINGER: What we find in following thousands of people is that many people who thought it was too late for them, who thought, “I’m no good at relationships,” found relationships at a time when they didn’t expect to.
sentences.zh: 沃尔丁格：我们在跟踪数千人的过程中发现，许多人认为这对他们来说为时已晚，他们认为“我不擅长人际关系”，却在他们意想不到的时候找到了人际关系。

sentences.en: We have a story in the book of one man who retired.
sentences.zh: 我们的书中有一个关于一位退休男子的故事。

sentences.en: He didn’t have a good marriage, and he never had friends.
sentences.zh: 他没有美满的婚姻，也没有朋友。

sentences.en: He joined a gym, and he found a group of friends who became his tribe, and they started socializing together.
sentences.zh: 他加入了一家健身房，并找到了一群成为他部落的朋友，他们开始一起社交。

sentences.en: And he wrote to us that he was happy in a way he had never been because he had these people in his life.
sentences.zh: 他写信给我们说，他感到前所未有的快乐，因为他的生活中有这些人。

sentences.en: We find people who find love in their 70s and 80s who never expected it.
sentences.zh: 我们发现人们在 70 多岁和 80 多岁的时候找到了爱情，但他们却从未想到过。

sentences.en: Based on our science, we can say that it’s never too late.
sentences.zh: 根据我们的科学，我们可以说永远不会太晚。

sentences.en: And if you think you’re never going to have good relationships, you don’t know that for sure.
sentences.zh: 如果你认为你永远不会拥有良好的关系，那你也不确定。

sentences.en: It’s worth the effort.
sentences.zh: 这是值得的。

sentences.en: People can make an effort.
sentences.zh: 人们可以做出努力。

blocks.html_en: GAZETTE: What steps should people take to start working on building good relationships?

sentences.en: GAZETTE: What steps should people take to start working on building good relationships?
sentences.zh: 公报：人们应该采取哪些步骤来开始建立良好的关系？

blocks.html_en: WALDINGER: We talk in the book about what we call “social fitness.” The reason we call it that is to frame it as analogous to physical fitness. We think of physical fitness as a practice, as something we do to maintain our bodies. Our social life is a living system, and it needs maintenance too. One of the ways you can do it is through tiny actions. You could think right now, “Whom do I miss? Who would I like to see more of? Who haven’t I been in touch with?” and send them a text, an email, or call them on the phone. You will be amazed at the positive responses that you get for this tiny action.

sentences.en: WALDINGER: We talk in the book about what we call “social fitness.”
sentences.zh: 沃尔丁格：我们在书中讨论了所谓的“社交健身”。

sentences.en: The reason we call it that is to frame it as analogous to physical fitness.
sentences.zh: 我们之所以这样称呼它，是因为它类似于身体健康。

sentences.en: We think of physical fitness as a practice, as something we do to maintain our bodies.
sentences.zh: 我们认为身体健康是一种练习，是我们为了保持身体而做的事情。

sentences.en: Our social life is a living system, and it needs maintenance too.
sentences.zh: 我们的社会生活是一个生命系统，也需要维护。

sentences.en: One of the ways you can do it is through tiny actions.
sentences.zh: 做到这一点的方法之一就是通过微小的行动。

sentences.en: You could think right now, “Whom do I miss?
sentences.zh: 你现在可以想：“我想念谁？

sentences.en: Who would I like to see more of?
sentences.zh: 我想看到更多谁的作品？

sentences.en: Who haven’t I been in touch with?”
sentences.zh: 我没和谁联系过？”

sentences.en: and send them a text, an email, or call them on the phone.
sentences.zh: 并向他们发送短信、电子邮件或打电话。

sentences.en: You will be amazed at the positive responses that you get for this tiny action.
sentences.zh: 你会对这个微小的行动所得到的积极反应感到惊讶。

blocks.html_en: The piece of advice I’d like to give is that there are some small actions we can take to enliven our social world. The other thing is to think about how you could make new connections, and probably one of the easiest ways to do that is to do something you care about or enjoy doing and do it alongside other people. It could be a bowling league, a gardening club, a knitting group, a political campaign, or working to prevent climate change. Just remember that when you do something you care about in a group, you already have something in common with the people you’re with. It’s a natural place to start conversations, and what we find is that when people repeatedly have casual contact with the same people, that’s the easiest place to start deepening relationships.

sentences.en: The piece of advice I’d like to give is that there are some small actions we can take to enliven our social world.
sentences.zh: 我想给出的建议是，我们可以采取一些小行动来活跃我们的社交世界。

sentences.en: The other thing is to think about how you could make new connections, and probably one of the easiest ways to do that is to do something you care about or enjoy doing and do it alongside other people.
sentences.zh: 另一件事是考虑如何建立新的联系，最简单的方法之一可能就是做你关心或喜欢做的事情，并与其他人一起做。

sentences.en: It could be a bowling league, a gardening club, a knitting group, a political campaign, or working to prevent climate change.
sentences.zh: 它可以是保龄球联盟、园艺俱乐部、编织团体、政治运动或防止气候变化的努力。

sentences.en: Just remember that when you do something you care about in a group, you already have something in common with the people you’re with.
sentences.zh: 请记住，当您在团队中做自己关心的事情时，您已经与周围的人有了一些共同点。

sentences.en: It’s a natural place to start conversations, and what we find is that when people repeatedly have casual contact with the same people, that’s the easiest place to start deepening relationships.
sentences.zh: 这是开始对话的自然场所，我们发现，当人们反复与同一个人进行随意接触时，这是开始加深关系的最容易的地方。

blocks.html_en: One last point I want to make is that nobody is happy all the time. That’s important to know because we can end up believing that if we’re not happy all the time, we’re doing something wrong. No life is happy all the time. Every life is filled with challenge and hard times. This idea about strengthening relationships is a way to increase our happiness, but also to build a safety net that helps us weather those hard times that all of us have in our lives.

sentences.en: One last point I want to make is that nobody is happy all the time.
sentences.zh: 我想说的最后一点是，没有人总是快乐的。

sentences.en: That’s important to know because we can end up believing that if we’re not happy all the time, we’re doing something wrong.
sentences.zh: 知道这一点很重要，因为我们最终可能会相信，如果我们一直不快乐，我们就做错了什么。

sentences.en: No life is happy all the time.
sentences.zh: 没有人的生活是永远幸福的。

sentences.en: Every life is filled with challenge and hard times.
sentences.zh: 每一个生命都充满挑战和艰难时刻。

sentences.en: This idea about strengthening relationships is a way to increase our happiness, but also to build a safety net that helps us weather those hard times that all of us have in our lives.
sentences.zh: 这种加强人际关系的想法是增加我们幸福感的一种方式，同时也可以建立一个安全网，帮助我们度过生活中遇到的困难时期。

content_html_zh:
哈佛大学成人发展研究中心主任罗伯特·瓦尔丁格表示，他们遇到的最大的惊喜之一是，让人们快乐的同时也有助于他们保持健康——人际关系。 该研究项目于 1938 年开始，是对成年人身心健康最长的深入研究，共有 724 名参与者：268 名哈佛大学二年级学生和 456 名来自波士顿的年轻人。 现在，该组织已有 1,300 名最初参与者的后代。 《公报》采​​访了沃尔丁格，谈论了他与马克·舒尔茨合着的新书《美好生活》。 为了篇幅和清晰度，采访内容经过编辑。

Q&A

罗伯特·沃尔丁格

公报：您书中的结论之一涉及良好的关系对于身心健康的重要性。 研究人员是否期望这是真的？

沃尔丁格：作为研究的一部分，我们跟踪了第一代参与者的整个成年生活——从青少年时期一直到老年。 当他们年满 80 岁时，我们意识到我们拥有有关他们身心健康的所有数据，这些数据是我们年复一年收集的。

我们开始思考是否可以回顾一下参与者中年时的生活，看看哪些因素最能预测到 80 岁时会幸福和健康。 我们认为 50 岁时胆固醇水平或血压会更重要。 他们不是。 对他们的关系，特别是对婚姻的满意度，是幸福和健康生活的最佳预示。

起初，我们不相信；我们想知道这怎么可能。 我们想，“如果你拥有幸福的人际关系，你会更快乐，这是有道理的，但你的人际关系的质量如何会增加或减少你患冠状动脉疾病、2 型糖尿病或关节炎的可能性呢？” 我们认为这也许不是一个真正的发现，也许是偶然的。 然后其他研究小组也开始发现同样的事情。 现在这是一个非常有力的发现。 众所周知，人际联系以及这些联系的质量确实会影响健康和幸福。

“如果你独自一人并感到压力和孤独，这就是破坏你健康的部分原因。 这就是为什么我们认为孤独对健康的危害与每天吸半包烟或肥胖一样危险。”

公报：是否有确凿的医学证据支持良好的人际关系如何影响身体健康？

沃尔丁格：有些人可能认为这个发现非常敏感，对吧？ 你问的问题正是研究人员所问的，即“这是如何工作的？ 关系影响生理的机制是什么？” 过去 10 年我们一直在实验室里研究这个问题。 有充分数据支持的最佳假设表明，它与压力以及我们的人际关系对压力的调节有关。

首先，压力是生活中自然的一部分。 对于我们大多数人来说，这种情况每天都会发生：某些事情会给我们带来压力，当这种情况发生时，身体就会进入战斗或逃跑模式。 当这种情况发生时，您会感觉到心率加快，血压升高，您可能会开始出汗，这是正常的，因为我们希望身体做好准备迎接挑战。 但当挑战消除后，我们希望身体恢复平衡。 例如，如果我白天发生了一些令人不安的事情，而我正在翻腾或沉思，我就会回家和我的妻子或朋友交谈，如果那个人是一个好的倾听者，我真的可以感觉到我的身体平静下来。

但如果你没有这样的人，很多人也没有，如果你被孤立或者没有知己，我们认为会发生的情况是身体处于一种低水平的战斗或逃跑模式，这意味着循环压力激素水平更高，炎症水平更高，这些东西会逐渐磨损许多身体系统。 这就是我们认为压力会削弱多个身体系统的原因，也是良好的人际关系可以保护我们健康的原因。

公报：职业和财务上的成功怎么样？ 它们和良好的关系一样重要吗？

沃尔丁格：当然，拥有一份自己喜欢或关心并且觉得有意义的工作很重要。 从事你讨厌的工作肯定会降低你的幸福感。 但我们从良好的研究中得知，一旦我们的基本需求得到满足，财富就不会显着增加幸福感。 一旦你超出了基本的财务保障，你的幸福感就不会增加太多。

同样，名声或成就——成为哈佛大学教授或获得诺贝尔奖——也不会让你更快乐。 也许让你获得诺贝尔奖的工作对你来说很有意义，可以让你开心。 但成就徽章和财富徽章并不会让人们感到快乐。 记住这一点很重要，因为我们会互相讲很多让我们快乐的故事。 我们整天从广告中收到这些信息，这些广告传达的信息是，如果你买这个东西，你就会更快乐，或者它们展示了人们过着美好而富裕的生活，这是幸福生活的关键。 事实证明这不是真的。

“我们在研究中发现，每个人都需要至少一种牢固的关系，他们觉得在需要的时候可以依靠的人。”

公报：你的书强调了与父母、兄弟姐妹、邻居、同事甚至熟人保持良好关系的重要性。 你能扩展一下吗？

WALDINGER：您需要拥有的连接数量没有规定。 如果您拥有家人所需的一切，那就太好了。 也许，你不需要更广阔的圈子。 但我们发现，关系的好处来自任何地方。 它们当然来自家人，但也可以来自朋友、同事，我们甚至可以通过与咖啡店里为我们煮咖啡的人聊天，或者与杂货店结账的收银员或邮递员聊天来获得一点点幸福感。 如果我们与这些人有愉快的联系，这些也会对我们的福祉做出贡献。

我们中的一些人比较害羞，而另一些人则比较外向。 害羞的人需要​​较少的人际关系，而外向的人则需要更多的人际关系。 我们在研究中发现，每个人都需要至少一种牢固的关系，他们认为在需要时可以依靠的人。 在我们的一份调查问卷中，我们问参与者：“如果你生病或害怕了，你可以在半夜打电话给谁？ 把所有人都列出来。” 大多数人可以列出几个人，但有些人，甚至有些已婚的人，无法列出任何人。 我们认为每个人都至少需要一个你知道会在你身边的人。

“我们的社会生活是一个生命系统，也需要维护。 做到这一点的方法之一就是通过微小的行动。”

公报：孤独对您的身体健康有何影响？ 您在书中写道，孤独对您的健康可能与吸烟或肥胖一样危险。

沃尔丁格：我们认为它是通过这种慢性压力机制发挥作用的——孤独是一种压力源。 我们进化成为社会生物，因为在群体中更安全。 如果你想想当我们试图在荒野中生存时，你就会意识到团结起来的人们能活得更久。 我们假设基因选择是为了变得更加社交。 独处是一种压力源；被孤立是一种压力源。 许多人在孤独时会长期感到不安全。 如果你独自一人并且感到满足，那就不同了。 但如果你独自一人并感到压力和孤独，这就是破坏你健康的部分原因。 这就是为什么我们认为孤独对健康的危害与每天吸半包烟或肥胖一样危险。 孤独与其他两个问题有着相似的生理特征。

公报：如果人们觉得在生命中建立良好的人际关系为时已晚怎么办？

沃尔丁格：我们在跟踪数千人的过程中发现，许多人认为这对他们来说为时已晚，他们认为“我不擅长人际关系”，却在他们意想不到的时候找到了人际关系。 我们的书中有一个关于一位退休男子的故事。 他没有美满的婚姻，也没有朋友。 他加入了一家健身房，并找到了一群成为他部落的朋友，他们开始一起社交。 他写信给我们说，他感到前所未有的快乐，因为他的生活中有这些人。 我们发现人们在 70 多岁和 80 多岁的时候找到了爱情，但他们却从未想到过。 根据我们的科学，我们可以说永远不会太晚。 如果你认为你永远不会拥有良好的关系，那你也不确定。 这是值得的。 人们可以做出努力。

公报：人们应该采取哪些步骤来开始建立良好的关系？

沃尔丁格：我们在书中讨论了所谓的“社交健身”。 我们之所以这样称呼它，是因为它类似于身体健康。 我们认为身体健康是一种练习，是我们为了保持身体而做的事情。 我们的社会生活是一个生命系统，也需要维护。 做到这一点的方法之一就是通过微小的行动。 你现在可以想：“我想念谁？ 我想看到更多谁的作品？ 我没和谁联系过？” 并向他们发送短信、电子邮件或打电话。 你会对这个微小的行动所得到的积极反应感到惊讶。

我想给出的建议是，我们可以采取一些小行动来活跃我们的社交世界。 另一件事是考虑如何建立新的联系，最简单的方法之一可能就是做你关心或喜欢做的事情，并与其他人一起做。 它可以是保龄球联盟、园艺俱乐部、编织团体、政治运动或防止气候变化的努力。 请记住，当您在团队中做自己关心的事情时，您已经与周围的人有了一些共同点。 这是开始对话的自然场所，我们发现，当人们反复与同一个人进行随意接触时，这是开始加深关系的最容易的地方。

我想说的最后一点是，没有人总是快乐的。 知道这一点很重要，因为我们最终可能会相信，如果我们一直不快乐，我们就做错了什么。 没有人的生活是永远幸福的。 每一个生命都充满挑战和艰难时刻。 这种加强人际关系的想法是增加我们幸福感的一种方式，同时也可以建立一个安全网，帮助我们度过生活中遇到的困难时期。
